book: 268 - Food & Philosophy - Eat, Think, and Be Merry
samples: Verene argues that cooking marks the transition from nature to culture, reading Plato's Protagoras myth of Prometheus (fire and the practical arts) and the Republic's claim that a city's first need is food as evidence that humans alone 'eat' rather than 'feed.' Tracing Greco-Roman banquets, Vico's account of Roman dining, and Brillat-Savarin's Physiology of Taste, he connects the ordered courses of a proper meal to Aristotle's view of imagination as rooted in memory and to friendship at table. He ends by mapping Brillat-Savarin's gourmandism onto Epicurus's distinction between kinetic pleasures (eating fine food) and catastematic pleasure (ataraxia, the settled well-being of good health and stored memories of shared meals).

Verene interprets Plutarch's Dinner of the Seven Wise Men, in which Thales, Solon, Bias and the others gather at Corinth under Periander and turn a plain dinner into a symposium on good government, household economics, and the soul. He reads their exchanges through Aristotle: Thales' claim that a ruler's happiness is to die naturally in old age is glossed by Aristotle's eudaimonia (no one is called happy until life is complete), the assigned-seating companions exemplify Aristotle's friendship of utility, and the pivot from politics to home management mirrors Aristotle linking Politics to Economics. Solon's Stoic argument that dependence on food enslaves the soul, and Thales' correction of the Ethiopian king's riddle-answers (virtue not God as most helpful), show the Seven speaking as philosophers rather than gourmets, with Epicurus invoked on death being nothing to the living.

Verene condenses the fifteen rambling books of Athenaeus's Learned Banqueters, where the character Athenaeus reports to Timocrates a multi-day banquet hosted by Larensius, threaded with catalogues of fish, wine, cups, courtesans and gluttons. He argues the sprawling work embodies dining as a two-part act of food plus discourse, and that its implicit ethic is Epicurean: Book 12's Cyrenaic doctrine that pleasure exists only in the passing moment (Aristippus) is shown to be historically superseded by Epicurus's modified hedonism, which ties bodily pleasures to ataraxia and even welcomes hetaerae like Leontion into the philosophical circle. Book 13's closing attack on the Cynics as homeless 'foul-mouthed gluttons' confirms the banqueters' preference for a regulated, prudent pursuit of pleasure at table.

Verene frames the two great cookbooks, Apicius's De Re Coquinaria and Artusi's La scienza in cucina, through a contrast between a 'Cartesian' and a 'Vichian' epistemology of cookery: Descartes' Discourse on Method, which discards custom for clear-and-distinct reasoning, is blamed for the restaurant chef's invented 'stacked food,' while Vico's New Science, which grounds knowledge in historical tradition, underwrites the trattoria and the home kitchen. Reading Apicius's garum and dormice and Artusi's health-and-economy motto (glossed via Aristotle's Economics as household management), he defends recipes as repeatable topoi like songs rather than one-off novelties. He closes by tying table manners to Rousseau's moeurs and to Socrates' claim in the Phaedo that speaking (and by extension cooking and eating) badly does harm to the soul.

book: 271 - Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy
samples: Davison uses St. Augustine's claim from the Confessions that only the present moment is real – past and future exist only as memory and anticipation – to argue that a father should stop missing his children's lives by fixating on past regrets or future worries. Drawing on Steindl-Rast and Thomas Sterner, he contrasts mechanical 'clock time' with quality-driven 'experienced time' and recommends process-focus over end-product focus, illustrated with lying beside his sleeping daughter Grace and dreading bedtime routines with his sons.

Allred applies Heidegger's Being and Time – the world as a meaningful context of projects, the hammer-as-tool example, and death as what makes projects meaningful – to contrast the father's world with the 'man-child' world of Seth Rogen's Judd Apatow characters (especially Knocked Up). He argues fatherhood reveals the fragility of all projects, using Plato's account of seeking immortality through children and Paul Celan's poem 'Epitaph for François' about his stillborn son to show that after a child is born the parent's world is forever haunted by the possibility of its emptiness.

Fink-Jensen, an anthropologist, uses narrative analysis and rites-of-passage theory (Van Gennep's separation/liminal/reincorporation stages) to examine how men construct the internal identity of 'father.' Drawing on interviews with first-time dads (Marc, Jim, Craig, Steve), she argues that because men lack the biological markers of pregnancy they feel alienated from the transition, and that Western 'couvade' activities – attending prenatal classes and appointments, hearing the heartbeat – plus telling birth stories function as rituals that cement fatherhood as an identity.

Barnwell argues that fatherhood can constitute the ultimate meaning of a man's life, answering the paradox that a meaningful life 'all about the kids' seems not to be about the father by noting fatherly acts are still the father's own freely chosen activities. He confronts Camus's Myth of Sisyphus – the worry that childrearing is endless pointless rock-pushing across generations – by insisting children, unlike rocks, have intrinsic value, and invokes the Sartrean existentialist idea that choosing an activity confers value on it (illustrated by his buying oatmeal for 'Sally').

Nease lays out a game plan for raising ethical children, using Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics – eudaimonia as a flourishing life, virtue as the mean between extremes, and the master-skills of practical wisdom and self-control – as the core, mocking 'character counts' posters as no substitute for early habit-formation. He folds in Kant's motive of duty, Nietzsche's will-to-power (glossed via Janet Jackson's Control) as the drive to master oneself, and argues empathy (Theodor Lipps' inner imitation), self-awareness, concentration (Husserl's foreground/background), and a respect for justice must be cultivated to 'stack the deck' toward a good adult.

Terjesen defends a distinctively paternal form of caring against care ethics' maternal bias. Reviewing Kohlberg's moral-development scale, Gilligan's justice-vs-care orientations, and Noddings' 'engrossment' model of caring, he argues these frameworks make it seem fathers like his own undemonstrative Norwegian dad don't care. He reconceives 'paternalism' (via Gerald Dworkin's soft paternalism and examples like Darth Vader and Bambi's father) as tough-love caring focused on the child's future self, complementary to maternal caring and distinct from the impersonal justice orientation.

book: 272 - Motherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Birth of Wisdom
samples: Lintott's editor's introduction argues that motherhood is a site of serious philosophical significance rather than 'navel-gazing,' organizing the anthology's essays around Kant's three questions from the Critique of Pure Reason – what can I know, what ought I to do, what may I hope. She recasts these as the daily questions of contemporary mothers (about knowledge, ethical choices like breastfeeding or lying, and existential/spiritual meaning) and draws on Sara Ruddick's 'maternal thinking' to insist mothers are thinking beings. It is a framing essay connecting lived mothering to canonical philosophy rather than to a single pop-culture work.

Sue Ellen Henry uses John Dewey's pragmatism, especially The Quest for Certainty and Democracy and Education, to diagnose her own 'quest for certainty' as a new mother mediating expert parenting books against her own instincts. She argues Dewey's rejection of the false dichotomy between knowledge and belief shows that a mother's home is her 'laboratory,' where experience is itself a form of knowledge; her La Leche League experience models Dewey's integrated, feedback-driven inquiry against the isolating authority of 'scientific motherhood' texts.

Amy Kind examines the pervasiveness of parents lying to children (her own 'Bad Dream Spray') against Augustine's and Kant's absolute prohibition of lying, Mill's utilitarian permissiveness, and Sissela Bok's principle of veracity. She applies Kant's categorical imperative and formula of humanity – treating persons never merely as means – to argue that because young children have not fully developed their rational natures, the Kantian wrong of lying is mitigated, while illustrating the debate with South Park's Kyle reading Descartes, A Few Good Men's 'you can't handle the truth,' and Seinfeld's George Costanza ('it's not a lie if you believe it').

Bertha Alvarez Manninen reconciles her deepened respect for fetal life (after seeing her daughter on ultrasound) with a pro-choice stance by deploying Judith Jarvis Thomson's violinist thought experiment and the real McFall v. Shimp bodily-integrity ruling. She argues that even granting the fetus full personhood, no one's right to life entitles them to another's body, buttressing this with Kant's formula of humanity that a woman must not be reduced to a mere incubating means, and calls for American mizuko-kuyo-style grieving rituals so 'pro-choice' is not conflated with 'pro-abortion.'

Kim Anno recounts raising an intensely masculine adopted African-American son, Zack, as a lesbian mother, using Judith Butler's account of gender and desire (from Undoing Gender) and bell hooks's We Real Cool on black masculinity to interrogate the social construction of gender against Zack's seemingly 'hardwired' boyness. She reads his gendered choices in toys, clothes, and music (Black Eyed Peas hip-hop, Black Sabbath's 'Iron Man,' the Rocky theme) and his racialized treatment through these lenses, contrasting his family with the rigid gender scripts of I Love Lucy and The Jetsons and her own parents' Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf dynamic.

Elizabeth Butterfield reads her exhausting early motherhood through Simone de Beauvoir's The Ethics of Ambiguity and The Second Sex, arguing that 'the ideal mother,' like 'true womanhood,' is a social construction and that a mother is 'freedom in situation,' never a mother 'the way a stone is a stone.' She recasts Beauvoir's 'serious man' as the 'serious mother' who flees her freedom into the Motherhood Religion, and invokes Sartre's 'condemned to be free' and 'Hell is other people' (No Exit) to advocate the honest, self-aware 'genuine mother' over inauthentic self-sacrifice.

book: 273 - Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail
samples: In this Foreword, John Rousmaniere argues that sailing's 'numinous' moments — like his own experience of stillness on a becalmed ketch mid-Atlantic, when the skipper cut the engine and the crew felt suspended between sky and sea — are paths to genuine philosophical truths, not embarrassing flights of fancy. He enlists William James's 'Varieties of Religious Experience' and James's nautical metaphor for free will (the passenger who volunteers to take the helm) to argue that such mystical feelings can 'team up' with reason rather than opposing it. He insists mystery and craft must work together: piety is no substitute for seamanship (Shelley drowned in an unseaworthy boat), yet competence and numinous experience nurture each other.

Patrick Goold's introduction frames the whole volume by applying Socrates' 'ti esti?' question to sailing — asking what sailing essentially is — and concludes there is no timeless essence (counterexamples like iceboating and windsurfing defeat every definition), so the reflective sailor, like the philosopher, must proceed without certainty. He then invokes Aristotle's notion of telos/final cause to ask what draws people to sailing's danger and discomfort, previewing the essays: Part I finds self-knowledge and virtue in facing peril (Stillwaggon, Jobson, Lebens on eudaimonia, Hutch), while later parts treat sailing as a path to flourishing through Zen, Stoicism, Spinoza, aesthetics, and physics.

Jack Stillwaggon recounts his 1965 voyage as a seventeen-year-old crewing the replica HMS Bounty from New York to Florida — fires aboard, thirty-five-foot seas, seasickness, a crewman nearly left to die — and asks why modern people abandon comfort to court danger and discomfort. His answer is that we face the sea to prove something to ourselves about our worth and abilities: like the paratrooper who stays under fire or the soldier earning his 'red badge of courage,' the survived ordeal becomes a cherished high point that adds meaning to an otherwise 'silly' comfortable existence, leaving him more at peace and expecting more of himself thereafter.

Gary Jobson, writing from a long racing career with no philosophical vocabulary, offers practical wisdom on generating the inner strength and courage to win: focus on the task at hand rather than the outcome, visualize the race, stay calm under adversity, and 'have fun.' Through stories of Buddy Melges, Ted Turner's Fastnet, and Dennis Conner's America's Cup comeback, plus his own collegiate turnaround under coach Graham Hall, he argues resolve (not luck) drives comebacks, and he treats leadership, mentorship, patience, and consistency as cultivated traits of character — an implicit account of the virtues a competitive sailor must build.

Crista Lebens narrates a C-Scow sail on an inland lake — preparing the boat, casting off, coming about, capsizing, returning to the pier — as a journey toward Aristotelian eudaimonia (human flourishing). She argues sailing demands phronesis (practical wisdom) as body-knowledge, that coming about requires the Greek 'middle path' between being 'in irons' and capsizing, and that competence 'cannot be faked' so sailing forces one to live 'in truth' (via Werth's and Kierkegaard's account of the crowd 'in untruth'). Using Borgmann's device/thing distinction, she casts the sailboat as a 'thing' that calls forth skilled engagement, unlike the powerboat as a 'device' of consumption, and links truth to the beauty of a well-trimmed sail.

Richard Hutch develops a phenomenology of 'moral presence' — an assertion of human integrity in the face of despair when nothing else can be done — from the autobiographies of solo ocean sailors. He identifies three pathways: technical finesse (Robin Knox-Johnston, whose 'God helps those who help themselves' pragmatism Hutch reads as the Taoist wu-wei, action through non-action), cosmic quest (Bernard Moitessier's mystical communion, slingshot instead of radio), and personal test (Kay Cottee's epiphany near Cape Horn, transforming terror into fascination via Otto's mysterium tremendum et fascinans). He frames sailing as tragic-comic drama with technology as a deus ex machina, arguing that doing nothing is often the zenith of value.

book: 274 - Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate
samples: Pendergrast surveys coffee's history to explain why the same drink has always drawn extreme praise and condemnation — from Sufi monks and the 1511 Mecca ban, through the Women's Petition Against Coffee and Charles II's 1675 suppression proclamation, to Postum's scare ads and modern epidemiology on cancer and birth defects. It is a historical and scientific account (caffeine as an adenosine-blocking plant pesticide) rather than a philosophical argument; its closest philosophical move is the closing 'you are what you drink' hypothesis that we demonize or glorify the beverages we depend on.

Austin uses the everyday sense that 'we need the bean' to introduce a metaphysical debate about whether we need God to ground ethics, framed through the fair-trade coffee case. He contrasts Erik Wielenberg, who treats necessary ethical truths (e.g., that unfair trade is wrong, that suffering is intrinsically evil) as brute 'furniture of the universe' and follows Kant in holding that we ought to be moral simply because it is our duty, with J. P. Moreland, who argues such objective moral values, our knowledge of them, and the normative pull of obligation fit a theistic worldview better than naturalism. The chapter presents God as the 'Necessary Ground of Being' behind moral reality without settling the dispute.

Phillips argues that there is something-it-is-like to be a knowledgeable coffee drinker, using Nagel's bat and Jackson's Mary thought experiments — but where the bat is 'fundamentally alien,' coffee expertise is learnable, and via David Lewis's ability hypothesis the reader can apply book-knowledge of acidity, body, finish, and flavor to abilities they already have. He then invokes Hume's 'Of the Standard of Taste' (Homer's enduring appeal, the Don Quixote wine-tasters) to claim aesthetic and moral judgments spring from the same refinable sentiments, so that examining your cup free of prejudice is, echoing Socrates' 'unexamined life,' something we almost owe ourselves: the unexamined cup is not worth drinking.

Geisz reads his daily morning coffee ritual through Buddhist metaphysics: the pre-caffeine grogginess and its transient relief illustrate saṃsāra and duḥkha, the First Noble Truth, driven by self-centered craving (the Second). The transience of the perfect-temperature cup shows impermanence (anitya), and the question of whether a 'self' pre- or post-coffee exists is answered by anatman — he offers three hypotheses (full self dormant, half coffee-cyborg, self created ex Coffea) then dissolves them into no-self plus dependent arising, where the cup and drinker are empty nodes in a web of physical, economic, and karmic conditions. Each intentional sip lays down karma that binds tomorrow's 'me' further into the cycle.

Hernandez contrasts 'dark' existentialism — Sartre's café-bound claim that hell is other people and that the self is imprisoned in others' looks (illustrated by Starbucks' Pike Place backlash reshaping its identity), and Camus's absurd alienation — with an 'optimistic existentialism' that finds meaning in community. Drawing on Kierkegaard's Christian love, Jaspers's 'encounter,' Marcel's turn toward the other (her Sweet Eugene's pregnancy story), and above all Buber's I–Thou versus I–It, she argues the coffee community (neighborhood boards, fair-trade activism, the neighborly cup) is an existential ground where isolated bodies-toward-death create shared hope by treating each patron as a Thou rather than a discarded It.

Parker defends the coffeehouse as an accessible venue for real philosophy through Christopher Phillips's Socrates Café movement (and Marc Sautet's cafés-philos), arguing that Socratizing — sustained questioning that offers objections and alternatives, not mere talk — makes everyone a potential 'Socrates.' Answering the charge that amateur café philosophy is mere sophistry, he turns to Plato's Sophist to note the sophist is the one who takes payment and has an agenda, so it is salaried professors, not unpaid Phillips, who resemble sophists. Framing thoughtlessness (via Nietzsche's 'oblivion' and David Foster Wallace's cruise-ship essay) as philosophy's true adversary, he endorses a softened Socratic/Nozickian maxim that the unexamined life is simply not lived as fully.

book: 275 - Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life
samples: In this Foreword, hunter and nature writer David Petersen argues that hunting is his best 'philosophy professor,' teaching lessons about life, death, and human animality. He casts predation and evasion as a 'sacred game' that sculpted prey species through natural selection, and invokes Aldo Leopold's ideal of restraint 'even when no one is watching' to distinguish true, process-oriented hunters from gadget-reliant 'Wannabee' shooters using bait stations, GPS, and motorized decoys. He warns that banning hunting would cause wildlife overpopulation, framing the human as an ambivalent predator: both 'good' and 'bad.'

Editor Nathan Kowalsky's introduction opens with his boyhood memory of his father shooting a whitetail buck and his own tears, using it to argue that hunting confronts us with life and death 'right there in front of your face.' He insists hunting and philosophy are not an oxymoron (mocking the Elmer Fudd stereotype against Socrates 'downtown'), casts hunting itself as a paradox worth philosophizing about, and previews all the volume's chapters, framing philosophy as 'thinking hard' about an activity that makes humans and wildness literally touch through death.

Ilundáin-Agurruza stages his essay as a 'philosophical hunt,' first conceding Peter Singer's utilitarian case that sport hunting is wrong because it causes animal suffering for trivial ends, then arguing hunting can be non-trivial. Drawing on Aristotelian virtue ethics and Ortega y Gasset, he defends the 'Virtuous Hunter' who follows 'Diana's Code,' handicaps himself for a one-shot kill, and feels for the prey — citing De Niro's Michael in The Deer Hunter and Woody Allen's Love & Death — while condemning canned hunts and demeaning language ('varmint,' 'harvesting') as vicious extremes on a continuum.

Opening with his intimate encounter with a wolf, Vitali argues that 'fair chase' cannot mean fairness to the animal — since a right to fair chase would imply a more basic right not to be hunted, conceding the anti-hunting case. Instead, invoking Aristotelian human flourishing and Leopold's land ethic, he relocates fair chase to the hunter: hunting is moral only if it serves the biotic community through conservation and lets the hunter enter the predator-prey life-death continuum. He illustrates self-handicapping through master hunter Milo Burcham stalking a distant muley with a recurve bow.

Kretz systematically attacks the claim that hunting is environmental, using the Ducks Unlimited Canada case. She wields Hume's is-ought gap to deny that 'natural' hunting is thereby moral, cites evidence that hunters remove the fittest breeders and eliminate predators, and rejects Thoreau's hope that young hunters 'outgrow' killing as counterproductive (analogous to teaching theft to prevent it). Drawing on Brian Luke, she presses 'the paradox of ethical hunting': the sportsman's code (quick kills, retrieve the wounded) shows concern for the animal that, fully realized, entails not hunting at all.

Cerulli narrates his path from vegan to deer hunter, arguing that the same ethic — the intent to 'do no harm,' rooted in compassion, ahimsa, and feminist critiques of domination — underlies both vegetarianism and his hunting. Confronting the animal deaths hidden behind organic agriculture (farmer Joey 'plugging' deer and smoke-bombing woodchucks), he invokes Carol Adams's 'absent referent' to explain why he had to face the killing directly. Shooting and butchering a buck himself, guided by his Buddhist friend Richard, becomes an act of integrity and refusal of 'forgetfulness.'

book: 277 - Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink
samples: Porn journalist Gram Ponante's foreword riffs on Plato's Allegory of the Cave, casting porn as the shadows on the cave wall and the viewer as both prisoner and fire. He argues that unlike the manipulated prisoners, the porn viewer actively projects meaning onto a deliberately thin surface — forgiving porn its fake 'MILF' and 'schoolgirl' labels because the images 'become what we want them to be.' Porn is 'a cave to be filled in,' and adding plot or realism only breaks the fantasy by making the images less available for projection.

Dylan Ryder (a working porn star) and Dave Monroe argue that being a porn performer does not necessarily lower the prudential quality of one's life, against the common-sense view (fed by films like Boogie Nights) that porn stars are damaged, coerced, or degraded. They reject Aristotle's claim that virtue is necessary for eudaimonia and, citing Kant's deontology and utilitarianism as theories that sever welfare from morality, distinguish moral value from subjective wellbeing. Deploying the 'Happy Slave' thought experiment and Ron Amundson's disability-welfare research, they contend outsiders' pity reflects social stigma, not the performer's own first-personal welfare judgment.

Andrew Aberdein traces the historical 'interpenetration' of philosophy and pornography — from the French book trade's 'livres philosophiques' and Diderot, d'Argens's Thérèse philosophe, and Sade, back through Aretino's courtesan dialogues to Plato's Symposium (the root of 'platonic love'). He dwells on the medieval 'Lay of Aristotle,' where Phyllis rides Aristotle like a horse, using the image to stage two readings: Aristotle's, that nature (and woman) must submit to the golden mean of reason, versus Phyllis's, that nature cannot. He closes with a paradox aimed at MacKinnon-style subordination arguments: if John Norman's Gor novels show philosophy is less persuasive than porn, then any persuasive argument for censorship must have a false conclusion.

Evolutionary psychologists Anne Gordon and Shane Kraus coin 'porngasm' and, via a survey of 264 undergraduates, argue that watching porn may make men bad lovers because porn caters to male short-term mating psychology and misrepresents female orgasm (which they estimate is 80–95% faked on screen). Men more than women infer that female porn stars genuinely enjoy the sex, and more viewing predicts stronger such belief. They explain the male bias through the correspondence bias (reading moans as real arousal despite the filming situation) and Haselton and Buss's error-management theory, whereby men systematically over-infer women's sexual interest.

Theodore Bach argues that consuming porn co-opts the mind-reading 'simulation heuristic' (the same process behind the Mr. Tees airport puzzle), so that a viewer like 'Max' watching Naughty Office simulates being the boss rather than objectively watching. This explains porn's popularity, the money shot (a prop that keeps the viewer inside the off-line simulation), and why heterosexual men watch penises — they simulate their own. Invoking Nozick's experience machine and extending MacKinnon's critique via simulation and motor-imagery research, Bach warns that simulating aggressive, degrading acts toward women may transfer those dispositions into the real world.

Casey McKittrick accounts for gay 'bareback' pornography — the erotic celebration of condomless anal sex and visible semen exchange (the reinsertion shot, gangbang formats like Dawson's 50-Load Weekend). He situates it against the pathologizing of homosexuality, citing Foucault's History of Sexuality on the Victorian 'invention' of the homosexual and Lee Edelman on queer sexuality as outside reproductive futurity. Drawing on Freud's account of loss and the death drive (eros and thanatos), he reads semen as the 'lost object' — 'brothers' milk' — and bareback video as a fantasy screen restoring intimacy severed by AIDS, animating the struggle between the erotic and the lethal.

book: 278 - Fashion – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking with Style
samples: The editors' introduction argues that fashion, despite philosophers' contempt for it, raises serious questions in aesthetics, ethics, identity, and political philosophy. It surveys the volume's contributors: fashionability as an expert-plus-masses property (Prinz/Farennikova), Zangwill's alienation thesis, Russell on 'cool' as aesthetic virtue, the objectification of women through Barbie play and sweatshops, and Singer's demand (via the drowning-child argument) that spare money go to poverty relief rather than trendy clothes. It uses concrete cases — Ugg boots, the National Airlines 'Fly me' campaign, Tommie Smith and John Carlos's 1968 Olympic salute, foot binding — to show fashion carries the zeitgeist and can both liberate and enslave.

Farennikova and Prinz ask what makes something fashionable, arguing through thought experiments (Calvin Klein jeans, khakis, Robinson Crusoe's leather jacket, the accidental thrift-store punk, Gang Green, the mod couple) that four conditions must hold: many people wear the look, recognized experts endorse it, wearers intend to conform, and they regard it as having aesthetic value. They distinguish being fashionable from being merely popular or 'cool,' show fashionability is relative to group and to time, and note fashion must change to serve its signaling purpose — the Amish are 'intentionally unfashionable.'

Zangwill argues that 'fashionable' is a relational, sociological property (like 'famous'), yet things also directly *appear* fashionable or 'cool' to us in first-person perceptual experience as if coolness were a simple, non-relational quality (illustrated by seeing 1965 Mick Jagger as 'groovy'). He claims these two aspects — the third-person sociological concept and the first-person phenomenological one — cannot be united, so the concept of fashion is 'schizoid.' Invoking Nagel on consciousness and Bernard Williams's charge of alienation in Kantian and utilitarian ethics, he concludes fashion involves a projective illusion and is a genuine source of alienation.

Russell argues that being 'cool' is an aesthetic virtue distinct from being fashionable: the fashionable but anxious tryhard 'Allegra' fails to be cool precisely because her studied effort to win social approval is visible, whereas figures like James Dean or Marlene Dietrich seem effortlessly cool. Drawing an analogy to happiness and to moral virtues like compassion, he treats cool as a *self-effacing* goal — achieved only by caring about aesthetic matters for their own sake rather than for status, the way a genuinely virtuous person is moved directly by others' welfare rather than by a desire to be seen as good. He uses a Simpsons exchange (Homer, Marge, Bart, Lisa on what makes someone cool) to show that not-caring alone is insufficient.

Hamilton defends a dual account of design — solving functional problems *and* improving look or feel through style — against both the reduction of design to fashion/styling and the modernist reduction of it to pure engineering, using the London Design Museum dispute (Dyson vs. Rawsthorn), the Citroën 2CV, Dyson cyclonic cleaners, and Pye's notion of 'useless work' (directly functionless work like a jewelled sword handle). Turning to fashion in clothing, he draws on Simmel's analysis of fashion as simultaneously imitation and differentiation, and on Adorno's account of autonomous art, to argue fashion can never be autonomous art because it is inescapably functional and commodified, yet still counts as an art with classic and ephemeral, high and popular forms.

Freeland analyzes perfume advertising — chiefly Chanel's mini-film campaigns for No. 5 (Kidman/Luhrmann, Tautou/Jeunet) versus the younger, jauntier Coco Mademoiselle ads with Keira Knightley — to trace how fragrance is sold 'aspirationally' by tying scent to lifestyle, romance, and couture. She examines male-fragrance ads (Bronson's Mandom, Chanel Egoiste, Old Spice's Isaiah Mustafa) and celebrity scents fronted by women of color, exposing gender anxiety, colonialism, and near-explicit racism in perfume marketing. Invoking commodity fetishism and feminist critique, she argues the ads manipulate female desire but do not make consumers passive dupes: blog parodies and critical commentary show active resistance to the fantasy.

book: 279 - Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal
samples: In this foreword, historian Stephen Nissenbaum frames the book's central puzzle by asking the reader to picture Santa Claus kneeling in the Bethlehem manger and feeling why the image jars. He argues Christmas began as a fourth-century compromise: the Church Fathers fixed Jesus' birthday on December 25 to co-opt Saturnalia and the solstice and to refute Docetism (the claim Christ only 'seemed' to have a body) by giving him a human birthday. He traces how the resulting tension between piety and revelry led the Puritans to ban Christmas and how the secular, commercial Santa of Moore's 1823 poem came to dominate the American holiday, leaving the manger and the sleigh perpetually unreconciled.

Editor Scott Lowe's introduction surveys the volume, using the disputed origins of Christmas – the December date borrowed from Sol Invictus and Yule, the Christmas tree from Germanic custom, and a Santa descended from Odin, Thor and Krampus rather than any Christian saint – to show how little about the holiday is settled. It previews each contributor's argument, from Hume-based attacks on the virgin birth and Aiken's denial of a 'War on Christmas' to Foucauldian readings of Santa's surveillance, the ethics of the Santa lie, and atheist or Festivus alternatives, positioning the book as a set of philosophical debates over what Christmas actually means.

Jurgensen and Southworth apply Hume's argument against miracles to the virgin birth, treating it as a claimed violation of the natural law that virgins do not conceive. They attack the credibility of the only witnesses, Matthew and Luke, noting their third-hand sources (Mark, Q, L/M), their contradiction over whether Mary and Joseph were married, and the mistranslation of Isaiah's ambiguous 'almah' as the Greek 'parthenos' (literal virgin). Invoking Hume's four defects of miracle testimony and his maxim that no testimony suffices unless its falsehood would be more miraculous than the event, they conclude a rational person must reject the Christmas miracle.

Theologian Victor Lyons defends the virgin birth against the Humean empiricist objection voiced by Dawkins, Hitchens and Harris. He marshals the creeds and Church Fathers (Ignatius, Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, Origen's reply to Celsus) and argues Matthew's and Luke's independent nativity narratives point to a pre-gospel tradition of the virginal conception. Against Hume's claim that a wise man proportions belief to evidence, Lyons contends experience is not an infallible guide and that ruling out the miraculous a priori is a circular limit on inquiry, casting Mary and Joseph as the first skeptics who nonetheless accepted an event outside natural experience.

Medievalist Todd Preston argues that 'Put Christ Back in Christmas' misreads the holiday, which in the English tradition was always a balance of Christian and non-Christian elements. He shows Augustine (in On Christian Doctrine) and Boethius (in the Consolation of Philosophy, guided by Lady Philosophy) licensed Christians to absorb useful pagan philosophy, and that this apologetic openness let King Alfred, Pope Gregory and St. Boniface repurpose rather than erase heathen practice – turning Thor's oak into the Christmas fir. Tracing the Old English 'Cristesmæsse', Yule/Jol and Modraniht, and the secular revelry of Sir Gawain that Wyclif condemned, he concludes an authentic Christmas keeps its pagan half.

Scott Aiken argues the conservative 'War on Christmas' pushed by Gibson and O'Reilly is illusory on both fronts: cultural Christianity has already won, and keeping nativity scenes out of public schools protects minority rights under the Establishment Clause rather than persecuting the majority. He then mounts a separate attack, claiming both Christmas myths are bad on their merits – the nativity (star that leads wise men, vanishing Magi, Joseph's pointless genealogy) promotes mere credulity rather than tested faith, while the Santa myth glorifies a slave-owning surveiller who makes goodness merely instrumental. He adds that teaching the false Santa story undercuts parents' testimonial authority to teach the gospel as true.

book: 280 - Gardening – Philosophy for Everyone - Cultivating Wisdom
samples: O'Brien's editorial introduction frames gardening as engaging core philosophical questions and previews the volume. It argues that gardening promotes a good life not through hedonistic pleasure but through virtuous traits like patience and a Stoic-tinged tranquility that ancient philosophers from Epicurus to Hume prized, and it invokes Kant to cast the gardener as a visual artist. It also sketches gardens as cosmic symbols (Pythagorean ratios at Versailles) and closes on Plato's Phaedrus image of educating the soul as tending plants.

Isis Brook argues that gardening objectively improves both the land (through composting, nurturing plants, and Warwick Fox's 'responsive cohesion' with wider contexts) and the gardener's moral character. Taking a virtue-ethics approach and drawing on David Cooper, she holds that gardening practices incidentally cultivate patience, humility, recognition of reality, care for others, and open-heartedness. She uses concrete cases—Sackville-West's white garden at Sissinghurst, her own failed Cerinthe and thriving ferns—to show how collaborating with nature nurtures these flourishing-related virtues.

Meghan Ray reads classical agrarian texts to show that Greeks and Romans invested cultivating the soil with civic, moral, and religious meaning. Through Hesiod's Works and Days and Xenophon's Oeconomicus (with its Gardener/King Cyrus), and the Roman Scriptores Rei Rusticae (Cato, Varro, Columella) plus Virgil's Georgics, she argues farming was portrayed as the only honorable, pious profession that builds character—diligence, endurance, justice—and sustains the state. The chapter connects horticulture to a virtue-centered vision of the good and righteous life.

Matthew Hall challenges the exclusion of plants from gardening ethics, tracing it to the Garden of Eden where plants are denied life and given only instrumental value for humans. Against this he sets kincentric alternatives—the Achuar mothering manioc, the Raramuri treating plants as kin, and the living apple trees of the Hesperides—and Albert Schweitzer's reverence-for-life ethic. He proposes gardeners offer plants three 'gifts': acknowledging their autonomy, giving them care, and giving weeds space, extending moral consideration to plant life itself.

Helene Gammack surveys the seventeenth-century self-sufficient English estate as a fusion of pleasure and productivity, using Schellinks's account of Bridge Place, Celia Fiennes's journals, and figures like John Evelyn and Sir William Temple (whose Upon the Gardens of Epicurus links fruit to health and tranquility). She traces dovecotes, fishponds, deer parks, orchards, and glasshouse exotics, and connects the modern 'grow your own' revival—driven by sustainability, food miles, and provenance—to that older harmony of beauty and use in cultivating food.

Jo Day uses archaeological and textual evidence to argue that the earliest elite gardens of Mesopotamia, Egypt, and Minoan Crete carried symbolic roles beyond pleasure. Assyrian kings like Sennacherib and Ashurnasirpal II displayed captured exotic plants as 'botanical imperialism' and tokens of power over nature and conquered lands, while Egyptian temple and tomb gardens (Hatshepsut's incense trees, plants tied to deities) served ritual and mythic functions. The chapter shows the ancient garden as a stage for status, military prowess, and religious performance.
